claims.claim: Epiphanius of Salamis was the bishop of Salamis (also called Constantia), the metropolis of the island of Cyprus.
Epiphanius was born c. 310–320 near Eleutheropolis in Judea (Palestine) and died in 403 at sea on his return journey from Constantinople to Cyprus.
He was elected bishop of Salamis in 367 and held the office for nearly forty years until his death.
Before becoming bishop, Epiphanius spent time as a monk in Egypt and later founded a monastery at Besanduk near Eleutheropolis in Palestine, where he served as abbot.
The Sayings of Epiphanius (Apophthegmata) is a collection of sayings attributed to Epiphanius that appears in the corpus of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

The sayings depict Epiphanius as a Palestinian who learned monasticism in Egypt as a disciple of Abba Hilarion, and who maintained connections with Palestinian monasticism while serving as bishop of Cyprus.
In the sayings, Epiphanius is shown upholding Egyptian monastic traditions of continual prayer against the abbot of his own monastery in Palestine, who only observed the fixed hours of prayer.
The sayings also connect Epiphanius with the overthrow of pagan temples in Alexandria and include stories about Athanasius and the destruction of the Serapeum.
The Greek text of the Apophthegmata is preserved in Migne's Patrologia Graeca among the works of Epiphanius.

Epiphanius was known as a strong defender of orthodoxy and opponent of Origenism, and he intervened in major ecclesiastical controversies including the schism at Antioch, the Origenist controversy in Palestine, and the deposition of John Chrysostom at Constantinople.
Epiphanius's best-known works are the Ancoratus (374) and the Panarion (374-377), a compendium of eighty heresies; the Sayings represent a different, hagiographic tradition about him.
